# Split a Chunked Text Stream into Line-Balanced Parts

> **▶ [Solve it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/questions/split-a-chunked-text-stream-into-line-balanced-parts)** — free, no card: a runnable editor, the sample and hidden tests, a judged verdict, and the reference solution.

## Problem

A text source is supplied as an array of strings, `chunks`. This array is a replayable stand-in for the original iterator, so it may be inspected more than once. Chunk boundaries are arbitrary and may cut through the middle of a line.

Implement `split_balanced_lines` so it divides the fully concatenated content into exactly `parts` ordered strings while never breaking a line. Balance is measured by line count. If the combined stream contains $$L$$ lines and `parts` has value $$p$$, then every output string must contain either $$\lfloor L/p \rfloor$$ or $$\lceil L/p \rceil$$ lines. Each output string is the concatenation of consecutive whole lines in their original order. Any arrangement of the larger-sized groups is acceptable. Always return exactly `parts` strings; groups assigned zero lines are represented by `""`.

```java
String[] split_balanced_lines(String[] chunks, int parts)
```

Line handling rules:

- A `\n` character terminates a line and remains attached to that line.
- A final nonempty fragment with no trailing `\n` is still considered one line.
- A final `\n` does not create an additional empty line after it.
- An empty stream contains exactly zero lines.
- All other characters, including `\r`, are treated as literal content. Do not normalize line endings.

Example 1:

```text
Input: chunks = ["hel", "lo\nwo", "rld\nfoo\n", "bar"], parts = 2

Output: ["hello\nworld\n", "foo\nbar"]
```

Explanation: The combined stream is `"hello\nworld\nfoo\nbar"`, which has four lines, so each output part receives exactly two whole lines.

Example 2:

```text
Input: chunks = ["one\ntw", "o\nthree\nfour\n", "five"], parts = 3

Output: ["one\n", "two\nthree\n", "four\nfive"]
```

Explanation: The full text is `"one\ntwo\nthree\nfour\nfive"` with five lines. The chosen layout assigns one line to the first part and two lines to each later part, satisfying the floor/ceil requirement. Other balanced layouts are also valid.

Example 3:

```text
Input: chunks = ["", "", "x"], parts = 4

Output: ["x", "", "", ""]
```

Explanation: The stream contains only one line, so one output part holds that line while the remaining parts stay empty.

Constraints:

- $$1 \le \text{parts} \le 8000$$
- $$0 \le \text{chunks.length} \le 75000$$
- The total number of characters across all chunks is at most 900,000.
- Individual chunks may be empty strings.
- The concatenation of all returned strings must reproduce the original content exactly, preserving line and character order.

Your answer should state the time and memory complexity. In a real one-pass iterator setting where the total line count is unknown ahead of time, explain why exact final balance may require buffering/spooling or a preliminary counting pass. Do not claim that already-emitted group boundaries can always be repaired with constant memory.

## Hints

<details>
<summary>Hint 1</summary>

First reconstruct the full text by concatenating chunks, then split into lines, and finally distribute lines across parts to balance the number of lines.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 2</summary>

Use a greedy approach: assign lines to parts one by one, keeping track of the current part's line count, and start a new part when adding the next line would exceed the average.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Hint 3</summary>

The edge case to watch is when a single line is longer than the average lines per part, you must still put it entirely in one part.

</details>
